items.titleEn: Arsenal Analysed: 5 ways we beat the Blues
items.summaryEn: Take a look at our comeback victory over Chelsea with our tactical analysis
bodyEn: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard netted the goals as we came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at Emirates Stadium.
But how did we overcome Xabi Alonso's team? As ever, tactical guru Adrian Clarke has taken a deeper look at the victory in N5.
Here are five big reasons we beat our west London rivals.
CLASSY KAI
Kai Havertz delivered a masterful centre forward’s display against his former club.
Producing three shots, creating three chances, winning 10 duels overall, as well as experiencing a team-high eight touches inside the opposition box, his numbers were seriously strong.
Yet they don’t do justice to his overall impact, because it was Havertz’s subtle touches, positional intelligence and clever movement which set him apart.
Often pulling wide on the right-hand-side, the 27-year-old made himself extremely hard for defenders to pin down or mark.
See his heat map below, to get a better idea…
Havertz also scored our all-important first half equaliser, driving inside from the right before drilling an accurate left foot strike inside near post.
Interestingly, it was the only Premier League goal scored so far in 2026/27 that involved a passing move featuring all 11 players on a team.
So, in more ways than one, it was a special moment.
It was also, of course, Havertz’s sensational dummy that paved the way for a wonderful winning goal…
ODEGAARD OUTSTANDING AGAIN
If we start with that glorious 50th minute effort, it is worth noting how classy our build-up play was in the lead-up that euphoric moment.
Initially we swept the ball left in smooth fashion courtesy of Martin Odegaard, Havertz and Riccardo Calafiori, who fed it to wide man Christos Tzolis.

Once our Greek winger cut infield (see below) Calafiori’s brilliant support run on the inside dragged one of Chelsea’s centre backs away, leaving a lovely avenue (between the red lines below) for Tzolis to feed a pass into Havertz.
You can see that Odegaard has run off his midfield marker, Reece James, and our intelligent German striker acutely aware, dummying the ball magnificently to take Wesley Fofana out of the game.
This left Odegaard free to despatch an emphatic shot past Emi Martinez…
This goal bore many similarities with Odegaard’s goal against Manchester City in the Community Shield.
On the same wavelength, the Tzolis-Havertz-Odegaard axis was served up another beautiful goal.
Our ability to break the lines with a progressive forward pass stood out as an area of real strength for us throughout the game too.

When you break down the numbers (below) especially with passes that bypassed Chelsea’s midfield (82 v 33) it is clear that our compactness inside the engine room was vastly superior to our London rivals.
The way we moved the ball forward, with speed and fluidity, between the lines was a joy to watch.
A FINE FULL DEBUT FOR KONSA

The Emirates Stadium rose as one to acclaim one of the best tackles you will see all season in English football’s top-flight, from Ezri Konsa on former Aston Villa teammate Morgan Rogers during the second half.

Pouncing on a heavy touch from the Chelsea new boy, Konsa, who was making his first start as an Arsenal player, sprinted across quickly to time his slide tackle to perfection, taking the ball cleanly from his Rogers.
The roar it was greeted with, was akin to the sound of a goal being scored.
That moment will have greatly adhered Konsa to the supporters, but so would the quality of his performance.
On his home debut the England international only misplaced two passes to register a match-high 93.3% pass accuracy.
In addition, no teammate won more duels, ball recoveries, clearances or tackles.
Up against a high-class Chelsea attack, Konsa was terrific.
BRIGHT SET PLAYS
We may not have scored from a corner or free kick in this thrilling 2-1 success, but our invention at dead ball situations was wonderful to watch.
The way we exposed Chelsea’s defensive set-up with two unexpected, low free kicks sent across the face of goal was supremely intelligent.
As you can see, Xabi Alonso’s side, marking zonally, did leave an inviting hole for Odegaard to feed the ball into…
And Calafiori was a whisker away from scoring, denied by the legs of Martinez…
Not long afterwards the Italian did score from an almighty scramble, caused by this teasing low Declan Rice delivery, that once again exposed fragilities in Chelsea’s game plan.
We may have been denied by an offside call, but this free kick and the one before were planned and executed supremely well.
On another day Nicolas Jover’s ideas would have been labelled ‘genius’.
RAYA PLAYED HIS PART
The stats will tell you Chelsea only created 0.39 expected goals from their 13 attempts, but that is not a fair reflection.
The visitors carried a major threat all game long, especially from fast breakaways.
Our last line of defence though, David Raya, was calmness personified.
Decisive when it came to claiming crosses, the Spaniard’s decision-making and handling under pressure was superb.
As was his distribution. In what was a very noticeable tactic, Raya was keen to release our forwards with early kicks out of his hands as often as possible.
The accuracy of that distribution was largely excellent too, finding Havertz and Tzolis several times from long range.
Our World Cup-winning stopper also produced a phenomenal reflex save to deny Estevao an equaliser late on…
On a day when every single Arsenal player performed very well, Raya was one of the undisputed standouts.

bodyEn: The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”
Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.
Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”
The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.
But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

items.titleEn: Angelinou Pedro signs first professional contract
items.summaryEn: The young defender agreed pro terms on his 17th-birthday
bodyEn: Angelinou Pedro celebrated his 17th-birthday by signing his first professional contract.
The young central defender has been with us since he was just 11-years-old, and marks a significant step in his journey by turning pro.
"It's the best [birthday]," Angelinou said shortly after signing his contract, "it's a massive moment for me and my family.
"It's taken a lot of hard work behind the scenes to get to this point, but I'm just proud because it makes the contract a more special feeling, it's another milestone.
"I joined when I was 11. It's been a journey full of hard work, learning and sacrifice, so coming through the Academy and now signing professionally here, it's a massive honour."
Our Academy has produced a number of top talents in recent years, with the likes of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Max Dowman moving into the first team since Angelinou joined us.
The defender feels that the environment at our Academy, which he himself has benefited from, is the reason for our continued production of homegrown players.
"You're surrounded by top players and top coaches, who force you to improve and keep working.
"I'd say all of them [inspire me]. Once you see Academy players playing at the Emirates, you naturally think that one day it could be you."
As well as our Academy graduates, our first team features some formidable central defenders.
Angelinou appreciates the value in having such fantastic role models to look up to.
"I admire both Saliba and Gabriel. Gabriel for his aggression, leadership and mentality, while Saliba is composed. I try to take things from both players."
Looking ahead to the season, Angelinou reflected on his achievement, as well as his hunger to progress and develop.
"It's been a good journey [so far]. I just wanted to have a really strong season, keep on progressing and being consistent, in training or matches, just to make a good impression of myself."
Everyone at Arsenal congratulates Angelinou on signing his contract and looks forward to seeing him in action this season.

bodyEn: There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.
The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

bodyEn: Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

items.titleEn: The Arsenal Foundation supports Nepal appeal
items.summaryEn: More details on our support for the Nepal appeal
bodyEn: Everyone at Arsenal has been deeply saddened by the devastation caused by the flooding in Nepal.

Our thoughts are with all those affected, particularly the families who have lost loved ones, those still awaiting news of missing relatives, and the emergency teams supporting communities through an incredibly difficult period.
We know this tragedy has been felt deeply by Arsenal supporters in Nepal and across the wider Arsenal family.
The Arsenal Foundation has made a donation to support relief efforts and is working with charity partner, Save the Children, on a dedicated fundraising initiative.
Save the Children is responding in Nepal, working with local partners to support children and families affected by the flooding and help provide urgent assistance where it is needed most.
Supporters who would like to help can find more information and make a donation here.
We will pay tribute to the victims of this disaster ahead of our UEFA Champions League fixture against Napoli this week, joining other clubs in UEFA competitions in observing a moment of silence.

items.titleEn: Arsenal marks second year of Together Against Suicide
items.summaryEn: Read more about our second Together Against Suicide matchday event
bodyEn: Arsenal Football Club has marked the second year of Together Against Suicide during our home fixture with Chelsea as we continue to offer a matchday mental health drop-in service, with a particular focus on suicide.

Having done the same in 2025/26 on the matchday of our 1-1 draw against Manchester City, we marked the game against Chelsea, which gave us an opportunity to reintroduce the service, show how it has developed this season and make clear where supporters can access help.

For this matchday, our objectives were to reduce stigma through safe conversations about suicide, increase understanding of the support available, help supporters access that support through the club’s trusted connection with them, and demonstrate how we show up for our supporters throughout the season.
The Arsenal Hub was the main centre, with representatives from Samaritans, the Premier League, the NHS and Arsenal, alongside Men’s Health Minister James Frith, taking part in the event.

The discussion at the Hub focused on the importance of partnership working and how football clubs can play a valuable role in providing spaces for mental health support - the role being that football clubs are uniquely positioned to engage with supporters through the trusting relationships they hold, but then having provisions where specialist support through trusted partners is available.

As well as the discussions, a specialist mental health nurse from North London NHS Foundation Trust was also based at The Arsenal Hub from 2.30pm to 7.30pm. Samaritans volunteers also engaged with supporters outside the stadium from 2pm to 4.30pm, who made 3,000 Arsenal x Together Against Suicide button badges available to hand out to supporters on the day.

As we got closer to the match, our Senior Social Inclusion Manager, Jack Ironside and Clare Sumner, Chief Policy Officer, Premier League, spoke to matchday supporters about the project, which s funded by the Premier League and delivered by all 20 clubs.

There was then time for Jack to appear on our special pre-match preview show, Live from N5, where he laid out the importance of the campaign, our work and approach to supporter engagement in this area, the struggles of supporters who suffer from poor mental health and our role and responsibility in this space.
For more details about you can get in touch and about our programmes, please visit our dedicated Together Against Suicide page on our website.

items.titleEn: ‘Relief’ of Premier League title has given Arsenal confidence, says David Raya
items.summaryEn: Keeper says Gunners ‘can beat anybody in this league’Arteta’s side have started title defence with three winsDavid Raya says Arsenal are playing with greater confidence after the “relief” of winning the Premier League. The champions continued their perfect start to the defence of their crown with the 2-1 home win against Chelsea on Sunday, making it nine points out of nine.It was a powerhouse performance coloured by a freedom of expression, which stood in contrast to the nerviness of the final months of last season when the team laboured under a weight of pressure and expectation before they beat Manchester City to the title. That was Arsenal’s first triumph since 2004 and followed three consecutive runners-up finishes. Continue reading...
bodyEn: David Raya says Arsenal are playing with greater confidence after the “relief” of winning the Premier League. The champions continued their perfect start to the defence of their crown with the 2-1 home win against Chelsea on Sunday, making it nine points out of nine.

It was a powerhouse performance coloured by a freedom of expression, which stood in contrast to the nerviness of the final months of last season when the team laboured under a weight of pressure and expectation before they beat Manchester City to the title. That was Arsenal’s first triumph since 2004 and followed three consecutive runners-up finishes.

The shackles were off against Chelsea, just as they have been for much of the season, beginning with the 3-0 win against City in the Community Shield. Kai Havertz and Martin Ødegaard scored the goals against Chelsea and provided most of the creative flourishes. But it was the ferocity of the collective intensity, the sheer physicality, that took the breath. Raya pulled off a stunning late save to deny the Chelsea substitute Estêvão. Arsenal did not deserve to drop points. It was an ominous statement of intent.

“Winning the league after that many years and after those years that you are so close … it gives you that relief and it gives you that extra confidence,” Raya said. “Coming from the three games this season, especially the Community Shield, winning against City, the way we played against them – that gives you extra motivation and extra confidence to play the way we want to play …
“Hopefully we can keep playing this way because we know how good we are. We know we can beat anybody in this league. Let’s just focus on the moment and be in the present.”

The most eye-catching aspect of the display was how Arsenal reacted to going behind after 77 seconds to a Morgan Rogers volley. They attacked in waves and created a remarkable number of openings before Havertz equalised in the 25th minute. The belief could also be felt in the stands where there was no panic, only bellowed encouragement.
The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?

“There’s things to improve on that goal [by Rogers],” Raya said. “We had to defend a little bit better, especially right at the start of the game. It was disappointing to concede that goal. But the main thing is the reaction that we had after it and the way we played. The way we dominated, the way we attacked, we defended.
“We know how good Chelsea are, especially in transitions, and the way the play is dragged back to defend. So it was a really important win.”

bodyEn: With 25 minutes to go against Manchester United, the Everton supporters had something to roar about as Jack Grealish made his return after rejoining on loan. The attacking midfielder remains universally popular thanks to his desire to entertain, getting the hosts back on their feet by creating dangerous situations within seconds of his arrival. Everton were limited in the final third for long periods as Thierno Barry sat on the periphery. If David Moyes is to keep his side pushing for a top-half finish, he will need Grealish to be a creative focal point. Will Unwin
Match report: Everton 2-2 Manchester United

There was no shortage of highlights from the new arrivals as Arsenal battled back to beat Chelsea, Morgan Rogers setting the tone with a well-taken goal within two minutes. Emi Martínez got a hostile reception on his return to the Emirates but, while he may feel disappointed not to have kept out Kai Havertz’s opener, he made a handful of excellent saves, a diving stretch to deny Bukayo Saka the best of the bunch. Ezri Konsa, on his first start for Arsenal, had the home fans on their feet after a thunderous slide tackle to stop Rogers early in the second half, the standout moment of a solid performance. It was Christos Tzolis who really took the game by the scruff of the neck, however, harrying Chelsea’s defence with mazy dribbles and driving runs forward. He also provided the diagonal ball which, via Havertz’s audacious dummy, set up Martin Ødegaard to score the winner, earning a first Premier League assist. Will Magee
Match report: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea

If Thomas Tuchel required a reminder of precisely how good Alex Scott is, the Bournemouth midfielder provided it at St James’ Park. The 23-year-old reads the game a little faster and a little better than those around him and his stellar passing range raised the tone in a game Marco Rose’s side really should have won after cantering into a 2-0 lead, with Scott helping to create both goals. While Newcastle’s manager, Matthias Jaissle, can be heartened by his team’s refusal to surrender and, courtesy of goals from Harvey Barnes and Jacob Ramsey, their ultimate collection of a point, for long periods his players found no answers to Scott’s questions. Surely a first senior England cap beckons. The forthcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain, Croatia and Czechia offer ideal openings for Tuchel to put Scott on the international stage his talent demands. Louise Taylor
Match report: Newcastle 2-2 Bournemouth

The omens don’t look good for Álvaro Arbeloa. Only twice before have Fulham started a top-flight season with three successive defeats and it ended with relegation on both occasions: in 1951-52 and in 2020-21 under Scott Parker. Arbeloa tried to concentrate on the positives after throwing away the lead twice against Crystal Palace and ending up losing to Ben Chilwell’s winner. His side looked dangerous in attack, with Josh King having already developed an understanding with the summer signing Gonzalo García, even if the Spaniard played a comical role in Tyrick Mitchell’s second equaliser. Fulham’s defending is another matter entirely: Joachim Anderson’s lack of pace was repeatedly exposed by the high line they deployed against Palace and Arbeloa must find a solution before facing his former club Liverpool and then Manchester United. “We knew that this month would be very tough,” said Arbeloa. “But I told my players it will not define our entire season.” Ed Aarons
Match report: Fulham 2-3 Crystal Palace

Several positives for Liverpool in Suffolk on Friday: Bradley Barcola showing off his lightning speed in his cameo, Ronald Araújo solid in the troublesome right-back position and Alexander Isak coming back to the boil with two well-taken goals. Receiving the most plaudits in post-match was Cody Gakpo, who appeared headed for Manchester City or Tottenham in the transfer window but stayed on to supply both Isak goals. “Cody knows how much we value him,” said Andoni Iraola. The confirmed exit of the sporting director, Richard Hughes, on Saturday brought assessments of a mixed legacy. Eventually, Isak repeating the form of his Newcastle days may stamp the decision to pay a record fee for the striker. Florian Wirtz, another expensive Hughes purchase, continues to receive similarly mixed reviews. At Ipswich, attention was drawn to his losing possession 22 times. It was left to Gakpo, whose purchase and sale were deals Hughes did not do, to provide Liverpool’s creative edge. John Brewin
Match report: Ipswich 0-2 Liverpool

Iliman Ndiaye enthused about working hard in his Manchester City debut after his £65m transfer from Everton. “I ran my backside off for the team wanting to get the win and you have to do the dirty side sometimes,” said the Senegalese forward, who was removed on 87 minutes, and brushed off how he might have joined Tottenham instead. “It was always going to be City. I wanted Champions League [football] and to play for one of the best teams in the world. I’m not saying Tottenham is not but when Manchester City comes through you don’t say no. It’s been a good week for me and topped off with a win. I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing.” Jamie Jackson
Match report: Manchester City 1-0 Coventry

There were plenty of questions for Fabian Hürzeler to answer after Brighton’s draw with Leeds, namely why it took them the best part of an hour to wake up. But, for consecutive weekends, the Brighton manager had the pleasure of lauding Malick Yalcouyé’s performance. The 20-year-old was barely known even by his own club’s fans at the start of the campaign, having spent seasons on loan at Sturm Graz and Swansea since joining from Gothenburg for a reported £6m in July 2024. He has since started against Chelsea and Leeds, excelling in an attacking midfield role. Hürzeler said: “He shows a lot of energy, a lot of effort, he is good in possession and out of possession.” The Brighton manager has previously flagged Yalcouyé’s physicality as an area to improve and it is notable just how slight he is at just 5ft 7in. The Ivorian’s confidence, eagerness to enter combat and close control are in no doubt. He could be the next player off the conveyor belt of young talent who Brighton sell for a vast profit. Ben Bloom
Match report: Brighton 1-1 Leeds

On the eve of Tottenham firing blanks for the third straight game, Roberto De Zerbi joked Allan Dixon’s bodybuilder physique could help them threaten at set pieces. Tottenham’s player liaison, who is Daniel Levy’s brother-in-law, moved up the pecking order again after Spurs failed to score in their first three league games for the first time since 1974-75. The club spent more than £300m this summer, Sandro Tonali the pick of the new signings on a blunt outing at the City Ground. De Zerbi praised Spurs’ spirit in the stalemate, epitomised by Tonali during a first-half duel with Dan Ndoye which culminated in a Forest corner. “I think it will be an advertising clip for the Premier League,” said Forest’s head coach, Oliver Glasner. “This is what the league is famous for and everyone loves.” Ben Fisher
Match report: Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham

Nilson Angulo, who scored for Ecuador against Germany at the World Cup, remains an enigmatic presence, at once robust and delicate, cunning and naive, deft and clumsy. At times, not obviously related to the game going on around him, he will simply stop, and waggle his legs around as though stirring paint with his feet. One volleyed flick with the back of his ankle to return an overhit cross to the middle was remarkable. He is a master of accelerating and suddenly slowing to create space, control immaculate, then at other times he will simply charge out of play. The only thing harder than marking him, perhaps, is playing alongside him, trying to work out if a cross is ever going to come. He is a magnificent agent of chaos, that is clear; whether he is a high-grade footballer is less obvious. Jonathan Wilson
Match report: Brentford 1-1 Sunderland

Not many teenage centre-halves play regularly in the Premier League, but the Australia international Lucas Herrington is quietly establishing himself in Hull’s acclimatisation to the top flight. The summer signing from Colorado Rapids celebrated turning 19 on Saturday by coming off the bench against Aston Villa to help the Tigers keep another clean sheet. Herrington is rated as one of the finest defensive prospects in world football and underlined his promise with a vital block to deny Tyrone Mings. In all three of Hull’s Premier League games this season, Herrington has featured from the bench and the Queenslander’s star should continue to rise throughout the season. The Hull manager, Sergej Jakirovic, said: “Herrington is excellent and has great potential, so all these minutes are invaluable for him. I don’t have any fear when he’s on the pitch and I believe in him 100%. Provided he stays healthy, anything is possible.” Ross Heppenstall
Match report: Hull 0-0 Aston Villa

items.titleEn: Loan Watch: Nwaneri and Setford start with wins
items.summaryEn: A closer look at our loanees throughout 2026/27
bodyEn: Throughout 2026/27, there are several Arsenal stars out on loan to gain vital first-team football, or to continue their development.

Ethan Nwaneri last week joined Borussia Dortmund on loan for the campaign and enjoyed a flying start to life in Germany on Saturday. Coming on as a first-half substitute, Ethan inspired a comeback from two goals down away at Hoffenheim to secure a memorable 3-2 away win in the Bundesliga. The 19-year-old’s action in the box forced a late own goal from Albian Hajdari to take the points back to Dortmund, who maintain a maximum record after two games.

Also making his debut following a deadline day loan switch was young goalkeeper Tommy Setford, who has signed for Stevenage for 2026/27. It was an excellent introduction for Tommy to League One football on Saturday, as his side came from behind to thrash Barnsley 5-1 at Oakwell - one of the results of the weekend in the EFL. Tommy’s debut coincided with his team’s first league win of the season.

Following a fruitful year on loan at Shrewsbury Town last season, Ismeal Kabia is now spending 2026/27 north of the border with St Mirren in the Scottish Premiership. Ismeal’s first four appearances for the Buddies have included tests against each of the Old Firm sides, and his first full 90 came on Saturday against Celtic in Paisley. Despite taking a first-half lead, Craig McLeish’s men were beaten 2-1 on the day - but sit third, with three wins from their opening five.

With the Swedish domestic season continuing through the summer, Charles Sagoe Jr has now made 19 league appearances for Kalmar in the Allsvenskan since joining back in February. An excellent loan spell so far has seen Charles scoop 11 goal contributions in the top flight, though his side were crestfallen by a last-gasp 1-0 defeat to Halmstad last weekend. Placed 13th in a 16-team league, Kalmar continue their survival mission with Monday night’s hosting of European hopefuls Djurgarden.

Moving over to our Women’s loanees but remaining in Sweden, Cecily Wellesley-Smith has also spent the past few months competing in domestic action in Scandinavia. The young defender has made 13 league outings for Rosengard during the 2026 season so far, though missed the 1-0 win at Djurgarden last time out while representing the England Lionesses side at the Women’s U20 World Cup in Poland. The youth internationals played out a 1-1 draw with Canada in Bielsko-Biala on Saturday, Cecily playing the full match. Further group games approach this week against Tanzania and Brazil.

Remaining at the U20 World Cup, Jessie Gale joins Cecily in Lydia Bedford’s England squad and featured for 13 minutes of the opening Canada draw. Following her impressive spells with both Portsmouth and Bristol City last term, Jessie has now headed north to Newcastle United, and will represent the Magpies upon returning from international duty in Poland.

Having signed a professional contract back in January, Sophie Harwood has moved on loan to Sheffield United - joining Jessie at WSL 2 level. The teenager started at the back and played the full 90 minutes on her competitive Blades debut on Sunday, in their league-opening 1-0 defeat to Leicester City at Bramall Lane. Newcastle and Sheffield United are set to meet later this month, though Jessie could still be on international duty.

bodyEn: We’re back, baby. So, so back. Well, OK, not exactly back. But back down the time tunnel, for a while at least, as on a powder blue afternoon at the Emirates Stadium, Arsenal and Chelsea produced an opening half-hour that felt like a throwback to prime Barclays of the early 2000s.

In that period this really did feel like a twist on a classic: spells of midfield murder-ball, stretched and flustered full‑backs, players hurling themselves at the defensive lines like the fall guys in a cowboy western being tossed out through the saloon-bar doors.

Arsenal had 10 shots in that period and played breathless, physically overwhelming attacking football. The game settled after they scored their equaliser. In the second half it became simply gripping and episodic, broken up by subs and stoppages, which is the current dynamic. Second halves: these are a problem. But Arsenal never really looked like losing their 2-1 lead.
The key to the day was that agreeably wild opening half‑hour, evidence that both teams have will and the energy to progress this season. Which will, in turn, be good news for the Premier League.

About last season. It was OK, wasn’t it? Quite a lot of demo-mode football. Games that were like watching someone knitting a scarf. Teams with such elite levels of defensive organisation the experience is like watching one of those police motorbike display teams doing a pyramid, while a group of men on laptops furiously study the data.

All very orderly, and disciplined. Just lacking in colour and fire. And more significantly, the higher gears that mean you might actually be able to run step for step with Paris Saint-Germain, or blow away, rather than slowly strangle, an opponent.

It is about balance of course, about releasing the urge for total control. There was a moment on 87 minutes that captured both sides of this. Chelsea were awarded a free-kick 25 yards out in front of goal: high drama, a moment to be seized, necks craned forward in the seats. At which point Danny Welbeck, on as a late sub, sprinted straight to Reece James as he prepared to shoot, looking like a man in a state of high alert, some vital mission being run. Welbeck’s mission turned out to be handing James a piece of paper and urging him to read it. What was this? Expected 87th-minute free-kick numbers? Forty-seven per cent scoring chance uplift high and to the left? Maybe it just said “Score, dufus”, in which case, more of this please. James studied it dutifully, then paced out his run again. And to be fair, if the note did say hammer it straight into Declan Rice’s head, then job done, great process everyone. But the overriding feeling was: no, thank you. Away with you, interventionist wonks, tracksuited control freakery. This is art. This is play, this is drama. Whatever it is, it’s definitely not time for a briefing.

The other thing, simultaneous to this, was Morgan Rogers walking off around the pitch and being barracked relentlessly by the Arsenal fans – “You should have signed for a big club” – but looking spent, exhausted and emotionally drained, after giving everything to that part of the spectacle that felt like the counterpoint to Welbeck’s note, the wildness and the energy that feeds this thing.

There really was nothing not to like about that start, which was all jam, all sugar rush. First there was the manager match‑up, a kind of Basque childhood romcom revenge drama. The league needs rivalries and sibling symmetry. It feeds off this stuff. Hmm. They might have to start jabbing each other in the chest a bit more. But it was still fascinating to see Xabi Alonso on the touchline. This was fresh meat for the eye: jawline, pecs, tan, elite smart-casual styling, and above all an effortless sense of aura. There’s a new sheriff in town. Even the sun had appeared, giving off a weird, dead September heat, the sky behind the stand a pale Hockney blue. And Chelsea scored with 1min 17sec gone, Rogers finishing on the volley with a measured, very deliberate grubber into the corner.

For a while these two teams just ran into each other. Emi Martínez was kicked in the head but got up and was still booed relentlessly. Arsenal had a goal disallowed. They produced one flowing full-length move, set up by a lovely roll and spin by Myles Lewis‑Skelly. On 25 minutes it was 1-1, the goal all Kai Havertz’s own work as he drifted inside like a gangling, bookish Arjen Robben then shot low inside the near post.

Havertz was also involved in the decisive moment, producing a lovely, and indeed deeply unfashionable dummy to put Martin Ødegaard in space in front of goal. It wasn’t even really a dummy, Havertz just dribbled his foot away, with no real feint or shoulder dip in the classic dummy style.

Arsenal’s fans are sometimes frustrated by Ødegaard. He’s not direct enough, doesn’t shoot, always gilding the lily, regilding it, taking it back to the gilders for another look. Maybe this is how you get him to shoot. Put him right in front of goal with time to see every option, run the numbers, and conclude, ‘oh, well, I really am going to have to do this?’

The finish was emphatic. After that the game became snarling and mean for a bit. Arsenal did enter one of their slow periods, taking the air out of it, killing the game a bit. But this was an excellent win against a very promising Chelsea.

A final thought. The question will be asked: why don’t Arsenal always play like this? Why stop with the rage and forward gallops? The answer is that you can’t. It’s physically very hard. This is not a computer game. They’re humans, with 90 minutes to run. The real question is, can you raise it again, take that 30-minute spell and store it away, keep it ready in your repertoire? If so, and on the evidence here, we really might have an Arsenal upgrade on our hands.

bodyEn: Mikel Arteta warned that Arsenal are capable of hitting even greater heights after the Premier League champions sent a statement to their title rivals by fighting back from a goal down to beat Chelsea on Sunday.

Arteta’s side were under pressure after conceding for the first time this season when Morgan Rogers struck early at the Emirates Stadium, but the response to the setback was outstanding. Kai Havertz equalised before conjuring a brilliant dummy for a rejuvenated Martin Ødegaard to make it 2-1, ensuring that Arsenal moved level on points with Manchester City at the top of the Premier League.

“It was an exceptional performance,” Arteta said. “I enjoyed every minute from beginning to end, and the beginning was tough. But the team responded in a spectacular way – the conviction, the determination, the quality. It was beautiful. It was a fascinating game.

“I think it’s an indication for us of how we are capable of ­performing at an even higher level than last ­season. It depends on how we maintain and sustain that desire, that humbleness, and continue every day to try to find a better version of myself and the team. We still have a lot to grow and a lot to offer. This is the ambition of the team.”

Arsenal and City are the only sides who have won their first three games, a statistic Arteta took as evidence that the league will be even harder this time. “It is going to be super hard, the margins you win games,” he said.

“We went to Villa Park a few days ago and it was really tough. Today again. We’ll go to Sunderland and it’ll again be so, so tough. We know every week is going to be like this but that’s what we prepare for.”
Arteta was delighted with an exceptional midfield display from Ødegaard. Arsenal’s captain looks fit after two years of injury problems and has started the campaign with three goals in four games.

“He feels, confidence-wise, I think one of the highest that I’ve seen him,” Arteta said of the Norwegian. “He has a point to prove from last season as well, missing so much football. Kai is the same. I don’t know how many times they played together in the last three years but probably not much. He is enjoying his football. He was running ­forward, having shots, creating for his teammates.”

Arteta, who hopes Cristhian ­Mosquera will make a swift recovery from a muscle problem, was similarly positive about Havertz after the ­German impressed against his old club. “He looks settled, he looks happy, in his personal life some great things have happened,” he said. “He looks fit, he looks happy and he is scoring goals.”

While Arsenal celebrated, ­Chelsea reflected on coming up short. The Blues were exciting in attack but defensive shortcomings led to their first defeat under Xabi Alonso, whose new team have conceded seven in their first three league games.

“My priority is to win games and it’s easier when you don’t concede many,” Alonso said. “This is something that we need to address. We want to be tighter, to be more clinical, more balanced. But this takes time.

“We wanted to compete, we came to win. We were not that far, but it went their way. We could have scored to make it 2-1 and you never know what happens. But the result is the result, I’m not fighting against that. It hurts. But this is the first defeat, it is going to be a long journey and it doesn’t have a big impact in our mood.”

Chelsea are without a clean sheet in their past 19 league games but Alonso did not want to park the bus. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” he said. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute and to wait and to make a long game. We wanted to be active, we wanted to be protagonists in the pressing, sometimes to go higher, sometimes lower, to have good possessions. And we have done many right things. We need to make it better.”

Alonso was optimistic that Moisés Caicedo is not enduring a long-term issue after the midfielder missed out with injury. Caicedo is yet to start this season and it is uncertain if he will be back for Chelsea’s Carabao Cup tie against Leeds on Wednesday.
“It’s about assessing the risk,” Alonso said. “Probably last week we took him on too early and I don’t want to make the same mistake again.”

bodyEn: Match report: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea

The first heavyweight encounter of the Premier League season was previewed in some quarters as the immovable object versus the irresistible force. Arsenal do not give an inch. Chelsea have been fun and free-scoring under Xabi Alonso. Yet that overlooked something pretty fundamental. The percussive force of Arsenal’s game when they have the ball and want to make something happen.

Chelsea landed a significant blow after 77 seconds when Morgan Rogers put them in front with nicely executed volley from the edge of the area. It was not only the first goal that Arsenal have conceded this season but one with rich narrative strands. Rogers was chased by Arsenal over the summer only to join Chelsea for £117m.

The story here was about Arsenal’s reaction. The sheer fury of it. For a blistering spell that culminated in Kai Havertz’s equaliser on 25 minutes, they threatened to blow Chelsea off the pitch. Arsenal’s confidence shone through. They had not lost to their cross-town rivals in eleven previous meetings in all competitions, winning eight, but it was rooted in more than that. They had too much for Chelsea and they knew it.
Arsenal FC have had a good day at two offices
Martin Odegaard
double quotation markBig game, tough opponent, really hard for us and we got there in the end.
Conceding early is never ideal but the reaction was top and I thought we played really well. It was a brilliant performance.
We showed our quality with and without the ball; I think the result reflects that.
[Kai Havertz] is a really smart player – he moves so well and takes so much of the defenders’ attention.
Ezri Konsa
double quotation markI felt at home from the moment I joined. Buzzing to make my debut at home and three points is the most important thing.
[On going behind] It’s part of football and what matters is how you react. We reacted fantastically. On another day I think we score three or four.
[On his tackle on Morgan Rogers] I thought: ‘If I’m going, I’m going all-in.’ It got the crowd going. If you get it wrong, it’s bad, but when you get it right it’s a good feeling.
Three games down, 35 to go. But the top two might be set in stone.

That’s a fine victory for Arsenal, who recovered from the shock of Morgan Rogers’ 2nd-minute goal to dominate a dangerous opponent. Kai Havertz equalised and then made the winner for Martin Odegaard with a gorgeous dummy.

Chelsea can take some positives, but they will lament a lack of precision and concentration in the final third. Yet they almost grabbed a point when Estevao’s late sizzler was beautifully saved by David Raya.
A roar of satisfaction echoes round the Emirates Stadium!
90+4 min It’s now or never for Chelsea Football Club FC.

90+1 min “I think your two Arsenal statement victories are the big ones but I’d put two against Real Madrid in as well,” writes Will Vignoles. “The leg in Madrid in the run to the final with that Henry goal and a defence led by Pascal Cygan, and then the Declan Rice game where Arsenal maybe ceased to be the punchline of European football and were taken seriously in the continent again.”

Was the first one a statement win or just joyously unexpected? Agree completely on the second though. In a way, even though they lost, the semi-final second leg in Paris that season was almost a statement performance too.
90 min Four minutes of added time.
90 min: Arsenal substitution Noni Madueke replaces the excellently Bukayo Saka.

Estevao charges inside from the right, lolloping Hincapie into irrelevance, and blasts a rising curler from the edge of the area. Raya leaps to his right and brushes it over the bar with his left hand. That is a seriously good save, the best of the match by a distance.

88 min James wallops a free-kick from 30 yards that flattens Declan Rice on the edge of the area. He gets straight to his feet, but I wouldn’t fancy his chance of doing any long division for next couple of minutes.
87 min: Chelsea substitution Danny Welbeck, once of this parish, replace Morgan Rogers.
87 min Arsenal love defending a one-goal lead and they have settled into a familiar 4-4-2 shape without the ball.
Joao Pedro turns smartly and is fouled 30 yards from goal by Zubimendi, who should probably be booked but isn’t.

83 min Rogers finds Palmer, tries to back up the play and is deliberately tripped off the ball by Rice. Palmer shoots wide from a tight angle, at which point Rogers kicks off with Rice. He’s got a point – it should have been a free-kick and a yellow card.
Instead, Rogers is the one who gets booked for pushing Rice.
82 min “Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game, where Arsenal got absolutely larruped by Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea, was definitely a statement of some kind,” writes James Humphries. “‘God is dead’, maybe.”
81 min: Chelsea substitution Estevao comes on for Joao Pedro, who had a frustratingly woolly game.
[Edit: what the hell was I on about? Estevao came on for Pedro Neto.]

81 min “I like the cut of Chris Finnegan’s jib (69 min),” writes Matt Dony. “Let’s found the Campaign for the Limitation and Inhibition of Tzolis Over Real Impact Statistics. Not sure about the acronym, though.
80 min Arsenal’s next four games are away from home: Napoli, Sunderland, Ipswich (in the Carabao Cup) and Brighton.
Chelsea are home to Leeds (Carabao Cup) and Hull before visiting Brentford.
78 min: Arsenal substitutions Viktor Gyokeres and Mikel Merinoi replace Kai Havertz, who gave a masterclass in subtle centre-forward play, and the potential matchwinner Martin Odegaard.
76 min A Chelsea corner is headed away by Gabriel as far as James, 25 yards out. He pings a sweet shot that is headed away with masochistic glee by – you got it – Gabriel on the six-yard line.
74 min Now my ADHD brain wants to know – and share – Arsenal’s greatest statement performances. Old Trafford 1998 feels like the ultimate; Anfield 2001 would also be high on the list.

73 min It’s maybe a little excessive to call this a statement performance from Arsenal – but it has been a compelling assertion of their current supremacy, even more so because they went 1-0 down inside two minutes.

72 min Saka’s delicious corner takes a couple of ricochets at the near post and is grabbed on the line by Martinez. He was already on his back, not sure why, so he was fortunate the ball came straight to him.
70 min The resulting corner is flicked on by Havertz and then headed across goal and wide by a Chelsea defender.
Havertz has been majestic today, the player of the match for my GBP.

69 min: Good save! Havertz produces a deft flick through to legs of a defender to release Saka, who curls a thrilling first-time shot from the edge of the area. Martinez flies to his right to paw it round the post.
69 min Chris Finnegan emailed to suggest the assist for Odegaard’s goal should go to Havertz rather than Tzolis. I privately agreed, to which Chris responded thus:
double quotation markCall it extreme if you like, but I propose we hit it hard and we hit it fast with a major – and I mean major – leafleting campaign.
Can’t we just keep yelling at that bloody cloud?
67 min: Double substitution for Arsenal Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi replace Riccardo Calafiori and Myles Lewis-Skelly.
63 min Palmer controls the ball deftly on the run and lifts a right-foot shot from 15 yards. It’s too close to Raya but Chelea are playing much better now.
Moments later, Raya dives bravely and decisively at the feet of Acheampong, who was moving onto Joao Pedro’s cute through pass.

62 min “Long way to go,” writes Colum Farrelly, “but there’s an impression that Arsenal know what they’re doing as a team while Chelsea are made up of skilful players recently introduced to each other.”
If it looks like a duck…
61 min Pedro Neto, who has been Chelsea’s best attacker from right wing-back, tees up Gusto on the edge of the area. He whips a first-time shot over the bar.
60 min: Double substitution for Chelsea Pep Chavarria and Malo Gusto replace Jorrel Hato and a visibly frustrated Romeo Lavia. Chelsea’s central midfielders are now Gusto and Reece James.
59 min Oh go on then.

double quotation markIt’s more than a little unfair that, when it comes to innovation, Sam Allardyce is mainly remembered for bringing the 568ml glass of white wine into the mainstream. He was the first to regularly play 4-3-3 in the Premier League; he was also one of the first to build cosmopolitan teams and to find marginal gains through nutrition, fitness, physiotherapy and data analysis.

Even on a micro level, he rarely missed a trick when it came to maximising results. So when Fifa and Ifab issued new guidelines for the interpretation of the offside law in late 2003, introducing alien concepts like ‘phase of play’, ‘active’ and ‘passive’, Allardyce’s brain became extremely active.
58 min Chelsea are having a decent spell of possession, perhaps their best of the match. A promising move ends when Acheampong’s cross is well claimed on the stretch by David Raya.
Arsenal break and Lacroix is booked for a foul on Tzolis. In fact, Tzolis has also been booked for waving an imaginary card.
56 min Palmer releases Rogers on the left. His heavy touch invites Konsa to make the kind of full-pelt lunging challenge that defenders love. He gets it spot on and the home crowd cheer lustily.

items.summaryEn: About the Arsenal Student course and NCFE qualifications
bodyEn: Why study an NCFE qualification?

NCFE (Northern Council for Further Education) is a national, educational awarding body that designs, develops and certifies diverse, recognised vocational qualifications and awards. NCFE is the UK’s longest-established awarding body, as well as one of the UK’s fastest-growing.

NCFE qualifications are available at various levels. Level 1 and 2 are equivalent to GCSEs, Level 3 to A-Levels, and Levels 4 to 7 hold the same status of achievement as a degree. Harnessing the power and resources of Arsenal FC, we can provide our students with a high-quality, holistic experience tailored to their individual needs and specific career interests through NCFE qualifications.
Level 2 NCFE Diploma in Sport

The NCFE Level 2 Diploma in Sport (Sport, Exercise & Fitness) is intended for learners aged 16-plus (year 12) and prepares learners for higher education and gives a good introduction to the sport vocation.
It is designed as a one-year, full-time course that is equivalent to four GCSEs (from Grade 4 to 9) and will provide the foundation to continue education at Level 3.
Level 3 NCFE Diploma in Sport & Physical Activity

The NCFE Level 3 Diploma in Sport & Physical Activity (Sports Coaching) is intended for learners aged 17-plus (year 13) and prepares learners for further education, apprenticeships or sport-based employment.
It is designed as a one-year, full-time course that is equivalent to one and a half A-Levels with the following UCAS points: P-24, M-48, D-72, D*-84.
Level 3 NCFE Extended Diploma in Sport & Physical Activity

The NCFE Level 3 Extended Diploma in Sport & Physical Activity (Sports Coaching) is intended for learners aged 16-plus (year 12) and prepares learners for further education, apprenticeships, or sport-based employment.
It is designed as a two-year, full-time course that is equivalent to three A-Levels with the following UCAS points: P-48, M-98, D-144, D*-168.
